lines.text: Earns 31% a year on all the money it uses
lines.why: For every ₹100 of shareholders' money and loans in the business, it made ₹31 of operating profit last year (better than 85% of Capital Goods). Past years: steady; recent trend improving. Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 15, weak < 10 (default rule, all sectors).

lines.text: Earns 24% a year on shareholders' money
lines.why: For every ₹100 of shareholders' money, it made ₹24 of profit last year (better than 77% of Capital Goods). Past years: steady; recent trend flat. Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 15, weak < 10 (default rule, all sectors).
For every ₹100 of shareholders' money, it has borrowed ₹1 (better than 64% of Capital Goods). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≤ 0.5, weak > 1 (default rule, all sectors).
For every ₹1 of interest it pays, it earns ₹19.5 of operating profit (better than 58% of Capital Goods). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 5, weak < 3 (default rule, all sectors).

For every ₹100 of reported profit in recent years, ₹108 actually came in as cash (better than 46% of Capital Goods). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 0.8, weak < 0.5 (default rule, all sectors).
₹100 of sales 3 years ago is about ₹203 now (better than 76% of Capital Goods). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 10, weak < 0 (default rule, all sectors).

lines.text: Profit per share growing 28% a year
lines.why: ₹10 of earnings per share 3 years ago is about ₹20.9 now (better than 70% of Capital Goods). Colour from the sector rule (PROXY): good ≥ 10, weak < 0 (default rule, all sectors).

valuation.text: Price tag: cheaper than its close peers (after adjusting for growth)
valuation.why: You pay ₹36 for every ₹1 of yearly profit. Colour from close peers (Capital Goods, 65 stocks): middle half 44.5–146, peers' PEG 1.78–5.82 × this stock's fair P/E 25 (growth 27%/yr) (band rule PROXY).

lenses.sp: Wants a large, steady, cheap company with a strong balance sheet.
lenses.vd: In Benjamin Graham's spirit: would see a mixed picture (2 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: Market value above ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Graham avoided small companies; ₹5,000 crore is our Indian translation of 'adequate size'.

ch.r: Current assets ÷ current liabilities ≥ 2
ch.w: For every ₹100 it owes within a year, it holds ₹184 of cash, stock and dues coming in.

ch.r: Long-term debt ≤ current assets − current liabilities
ch.v: Long-term debt ₹39 cr vs working capital ₹6,695 cr
ch.w: Graham wanted the short-term cushion alone to be able to repay long-term loans.

ch.n: A profit every year for 10 years
ch.r: Positive earnings in each of the last 10 years
ch.v: Profit in all 4 yrs we have
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see; the earlier years are not in the free data.

ch.r: Dividends every year for 20 years (India: 10 years)
ch.w: A gap of about 31 months without a dividend (2016-11 to 2019-06).

ch.n: Earnings per share up a third in 10 years
ch.r: EPS +33% over 10 years (3-year averages at each end)
ch.w: EPS (average of the first 2 vs last 2 years we have) moved +53%.

ch.r: PE ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
ch.w: You pay ₹52 for every ₹1 of average yearly profit over the last 3 yrs.
You pay ₹9.32 for every ₹1 of net worth.

ch.r: Price < √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share)
ch.w: With EPS ₹209.5 and book value ₹797 per share, Graham's ceiling price is ₹1,938.

lenses.st: Wonderful business at a fair price
lenses.sp: Wants a simple business with a lasting edge, high returns without debt, and trustworthy managers.
lenses.vd: In Warren Buffett's spirit: a great business, and the price passes both this lens's own price test and the fair-value check (₹7,429 vs fair value ₹6,736).

ch.r: Could you explain how it makes money in two sentences?
q: What does it sell, and to whom?
Will people still need this in 10 years?

ch.r: A lasting edge: brand, low cost, network or switching costs
q: Why can't a well-funded rival copy it?
Has it kept high returns through bad years?

ch.r: ROE ≥ 15% in at least 8 of the last 10 years, with debt-to-equity < 0.5
ch.w: Strong in 4 of the 4 yrs we can see.

ch.r: No loss in 10 years
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see.

ch.n: Doesn't eat its cash in capex
ch.r: Capex < 50% of operating cash flow (5-year sum)
ch.v: Capex was 45% of cash from operations over 4 yrs
ch.w: Of every ₹100 of cash the business brought in, ₹45 went back into plant and equipment.

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have
ch.w: Your slice of the company hasn't been shrunk by new share issues.

ch.r: Candid, sensible with capital, no governance red flags
ch.v: 0 red flags, 1 to check (checked: auditor changes, CFO/KMP changes, credit ratings, SEBI orders, promoter holding, pledge).
ch.w: Our automatic checks are a starting point only.
q: Do they admit mistakes in the annual report letter?
Have past acquisitions and capex paid off?

ch.n: Bought with a margin of safety
ch.r: Price ≥ 25% below estimated intrinsic value
ch.w: Needs the fair-value (DCF) estimate, which arrives in Stage 4.

lenses.st: Great business at a fair price; invert
lenses.sp: Prefers a great business at a fair price, and first asks how the investment could fail.
lenses.vd: In Charlie Munger's spirit: a great business, and the price passes both this lens's own price test and the fair-value check (₹7,429 vs fair value ₹6,736).

ch.r: Average ROCE ≥ 20% over 5 years
ch.w: For every ₹100 in the business it earned about ₹26 a year.

ch.r: PEG (PE ÷ EPS growth) below 2
ch.w: PE 35.5 against EPS growth of 27.9% a year.

ch.r: Promoters own ≥ 25% and have pledged none
ch.w: Owners with lots of their own money in the shares, unborrowed against, tend to act like you would.

ch.n: Invert: how could this go wrong?
ch.r: List the ways you could lose money before the reasons to buy
ch.v: Starter list from our checks: Check: an auditor change in the last 3 years
q: What would make profits halve?
What would a short-seller say?

ch.r: Only invest in what you truly understand
q: Could you explain this business to a 12-year-old in 2 minutes?

lenses.st: Growth at a reasonable price · type: Fast grower
lenses.sp: First sorts the company by type (this one looks like a fast grower), then wants growth at a sensible PEG with low debt.
lenses.vd: In Peter Lynch's spirit: would see a mixed picture (2 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: PEG < 1 attractive, ~1 fair, ≥ 2 expensive
ch.w: PE 35.5 divided by EPS growth 27.9% a year (growth measured over 3 yrs).

ch.r: Debt-to-equity below 0.35
ch.w: ₹1 borrowed for every ₹100 of shareholders' money.

ch.r: EPS growth 20–25% a year
ch.w: Lynch liked 20–25%; much faster is hard to keep up and often over-priced.

ch.r: Inventory should not grow faster than sales
ch.w: Unsold goods rising faster than sales can mean demand is weakening.

ch.r: Insider buying is a green flag
ch.w: No insider trades disclosed to NSE in the last 12 months.

ch.r: A buyback is a green flag
ch.w: No buyback in the last 3 years (not a negative).

ch.n: Not a hot stock in a hot industry
ch.r: Avoid what everyone is excited about
q: Is this stock being talked about everywhere?
Has it more than doubled in a year on hopes rather than profits?

lenses.st: Outstanding growth companies, held for years
lenses.sp: Pays up for long growth runways, rising margins and candid, capable managers.
lenses.vd: In Philip Fisher's spirit: would likely find a lot to like (2 checks use fewer years than the rule needs).

ch.r: Sales growth ≥ 10% a year for many years
ch.w: Fisher wanted products with room for years of sales growth.

ch.r: Steady R&D and new products
ch.w: R&D spending isn't in the free data; check the annual report (pharma: R&D 6–10% of sales).

ch.r: Profit margin in the top 40% of its sector
ch.w: Fisher looked for companies earning more on each rupee of sales than rivals.

ch.r: Operating margin flat or rising over the years
ch.w: Fisher wanted managers working to lift margins.

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have
ch.w: Your slice of the company hasn't been shrunk by new share issues.

ch.r: Low staff turnover, no long strikes
q: Any strikes or high attrition mentioned in the annual report?

ch.r: Management talks openly about problems
q: In a bad quarter, did the concall explain why, or only blame the market?

ch.r: Ask customers, suppliers and competitors
q: What do people who use or sell its products say?

lenses.sp: Ranks every company on 'cheap' and 'good' and buys the best combined ranks.
lenses.vd: In Joel Greenblatt's spirit: would probably pass.

ch.r: Earnings yield (EBIT ÷ EV) in the top 30%
ch.w: The business earns ₹4.1 of operating profit a year for every ₹100 you'd pay for all of it (shares + debt − cash).

ch.r: EBIT ÷ (working capital + net fixed assets) in the top 30%
ch.w: Every ₹100 tied up in plant and working capital earns ₹33 of operating profit.

ch.n: Near the top of the Magic Formula list
ch.r: Combined rank (earnings-yield rank + return rank) in the top 10%
ch.w: Greenblatt's method (STATED) buys the best 20–30 combined ranks; 'top 10%' is our cut-off.

lenses.sp: Nine quick tests of whether the business got healthier this year than last.
lenses.vd: In Piotroski F-score's spirit: would see a mixed picture.

ch.r: Return on assets above zero
ch.w: Made a profit on its assets last year.

ch.r: Operating cash flow above zero
ch.w: The business brought in real cash.

ch.r: ROA higher than the year before
ch.w: Getting more profit out of its assets.

ch.r: Operating cash flow > net profit
ch.w: Profits backed by cash, not just accounting entries.

ch.r: Long-term debt ÷ assets lower than last year
ch.w: Less reliance on long-term loans.

ch.r: Current ratio higher than last year
ch.w: A thicker short-term cushion.

ch.r: Gross margin higher than last year
ch.w: Keeps more of each sale after direct costs.

ch.r: Share count not higher than last year
ch.w: Owners weren't diluted.

ch.r: Sales ÷ assets higher than last year
ch.w: Squeezing more sales out of what it owns.

lenses.st: Small, ambitious companies with big markets
lenses.sp: Looks for small companies run by experienced, ambitious people in huge markets – and patience.
lenses.vd: Too big for the SMILE style: Kedia looks for companies under ₹5,000 crore – so this lens doesn't fit, whatever the other answers.

ch.r: Market value under ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Kedia hunts small companies with room to grow many times over.

ch.r: Management with a proven record in this business
q: How long have the leaders run this business? What did they build before?

ch.r: Clear, ambitious growth plans
q: Do they state a 3–5 year target? Is it believable?

ch.r: Big, growing market to sell into
q: How big could sales be if they win a fair share?

ch.r: Willing to hold for years
q: Would you hold through a 40% fall?

ch.r: Pledged promoter shares are a red flag
ch.w: Pledged shares can be sold by lenders in a fall, pushing the price down further.

ch.r: No SEBI orders, auditor exits or similar red flags

ch.r: Average ROCE ≥ 15%

ch.r: No management red flags in our automatic checks
ch.v: 0 red flags, 1 to check (checked: auditor changes, CFO/KMP changes, credit ratings, SEBI orders, promoter holding, pledge).

ch.r: EPS growth > 15% a year over 5 years

ch.r: Can it keep this up for 10+ years?
ch.v: ROCE over the years we have: steady
q: What protects it from competition for the next decade?

ch.r: PEG < 1.5
ch.w: Price compared with growth.

lens_sum: Quality strong, price near fair value ₹6,736

sty.why: ROCE 22%+ in all 4 years we have, almost no debt, sales steady; Lynch-type fast grower (EPS growth 27.9% a year)

cw: 2 of 4 methods within ±25% of the fair value

rs.t: Earns 31% a year on all the money it uses – better than 85% of Capital Goods
Earns 24% a year on shareholders' money – better than 77% of Capital Goods
Sales growing 27% a year – better than 76% of Capital Goods
Profit per share growing 28% a year – better than 70% of Capital Goods
Price is below its 200-day average (₹8,474) – long-term trend down; 12-1 month return +1% (better than 59% of its sector)

v4.ll: Passes Buffett, Munger, Fisher, Agrawal, Mukherjea-style checks; fails Greenblatt, Kedia-style checks
ch: Drops to Hold if the quality score falls below 70 (now 77); to Avoid below 50.

Buy zone: below ₹6,175 (25% under the relative value ₹8,234, ⚖️ Balanced view), if the view's own conditions hold, confidence is Medium or High and the trend is up. Accumulate zone: ₹5,726–₹7,746 (consensus ₹6,736).
Moves to Trim above ₹8,757 (30% over fair value).

Any new serious red flag (auditor resigns mid-term, pledge above 25%, SEBI order, negative net worth, weak cash conversion together with high accruals, distress with interest cover below 1.5×) moves it straight to Avoid.

va.pw: Fast growers: 3-stage cash-flow forecast on owner earnings and earnings power, plus Lynch's PEG, peer PE and own PE band.

in.g_src: lower of sales 26.6%/yr and EPS 27.9%/yr, capped at 25%
in.stages: years 1–5 at 25.0%, years 6–10 fading to 6.0%, then 6.0% for ever

rdcf.w: Today's price assumes the cash base grows about 35% a year for 5 years (then slowing to 6%); the business grew about 27% a year recently.

epv.n: Floor check: what today's normal profit is worth if it never grew. Shown, not counted.

ddm.n: Floor check: all future dividends at a 17% payout. Shown, not counted.

mid_ev_ebitda.pa: 4 yrs of margins (a full cycle is 7–10)

sotp.w: Needs segment / listed-stake data (Stage 5 Company Reader); holding-company discount 20–40% (PROXY) will apply.

nav.w: Needs land bank / investment values from annual reports (Stage 5).

replacement.w: Needs capacity (tonnes) and today's cost per tonne from investor presentations (Stage 5).

story.what_it_does: Polycab makes wires and cables, which drive most of its sales, plus consumer electrical products (FMEG, such as solar and fans) and runs engineering projects (EPC). In FY26 wires and cables revenue was about ₹252 billion, up 33%, and about 5% of revenue comes from exports.
story.plans: Management plans a capex programme of at least ₹60 billion over five years (Project Spring), with annual capex of ₹12-16 billion through FY30. Targets by FY30 include an FMEG EBITDA margin of 8-10%, exports at 10% of revenue and a 30% dividend payout. It also plans to commission an EHV cable plant in FY28.
story.moat: The notes show scale and a strong balance sheet: record revenue of ₹288.8 billion in FY26 and net cash of ₹45.2 billion at September 2026. Margins in wires and cables stayed in the 12-14% range even as copper prices swung. However, the notes also say a new entrant, UltraTech, is reportedly pricing 10-15% lower, and management would not give market share figures.

scenarios.story: Revenue growth stays very strong, as in Q2 FY27 (up 53%), with FMEG revenue up 124% and a 10.1% margin. Net cash keeps building and the company funds its expansion and exports target from its own cash.
signals_to_watch: FMEG growth versus the industry at 1.5-2x and EBITDA margin staying at 8-10%
Export share moving from about 5% toward the 10% target as Middle East and US disruptions ease

scenarios.story: Growth stays healthy but cools as the copper-driven price rise and channel stocking fade. Wires and cables margins settle in the guided 11-13% range, and working capital days rise back to 45-50 from 11 days.
signals_to_watch: Cable and wire volume growth, which was only low to mid single digits in Q1 FY27
Working capital cycle moving back toward 45-50 days from 11 days

scenarios.story: Falling copper prices cause channel destocking, and cheaper competitors take share in wires. Geopolitical disruption keeps hurting exports and EPC revenue keeps shrinking.
